newsitem.title: INDIA: India to begin trial run for global pepper exchange.
newsitem.headline: India to begin trial run for global pepper exchange.

text.p: India plans to begin trial runs next week ahead of the start of the country's first international futures exchange for pepper by the end of April, officials said on Tuesday.
"There is good progress. Our expectation is to start (the exchange) by the end of April," Taranath Vidyasagar, President of the India Pepper and Spices Trade Association (IPSTA), told Reuters.
In February the Food Ministry announced that the country's first International Pepper Futures Exchange and clearing house would start functioning at Kochi in the southern state of Kerala by April.

India's cabinet decided in the second half of 1995 to upgrade the domestic futures commodity exchange, run by IPSTA in Kochi into an international exchange. The domestic exchange has 140 members and the annual volume of trade is about six billion rupees ($168 million).
"Mock runs at the pepper exchange will start next week," Vidyasagar said.
He said the mock runs would test the software systems and ensure trading was properly recorded. "We will see if the margining (trading) system as such is complete or not."
Vidyasagar said IPSTA would next week circulate details of the exchange internationally but does not plan a cut-off date for membership to the exchange.
"We have not put any limit on members. Let us see how many come through," he said.
He expects trading members from Rotterdam in the Netherlands, the United States, Germany, Britain and Singapore to join the first international exchange for pepper.
"Initially the volume will be low but it should pick up," Vidyasagar said.

Government officials said the exchange and clearing house will have a stabilising influence on forward trading in pepper by acting as a mechanism for ensuring steady stock on a regulated price to international buyers.

Analysts say India, which has opened its economy after decades of socialist controls, has developed cold feet on introducing commodity futures trading due to the conflicting interests of its 15-party centre-left coalition government.

The previous Congress party government had in 1993 decided to revive futures trade, which fell into disfavour three decades ago. An official committee has recommended futures trading in cotton, oilseeds and silver, gold and sugar.
Currently futures trading is allowed in castorseed, hessian, gur (jaggery), potatoes, turmeric and pepper.
India also plans to set up an international Castor Oil Futures Exchange.

Officials of the Kochi-based Spices Board said the government's role would be to ensure that there were no artificial barriers to trade and no shortages due to speculation. "We are only promoting and supporting the concept. It is our responsibility to see that it runs properly," said K.P.G. Menon, a Spices Board official.
India annually produces about one-third of the world's total pepper output of 180,000 tonnes. The other major producers include Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam.
India annually exports about 30,000 tonnes of pepper mainly to the United States, Europe and Japan. The remainder is consumed domestically.
Pepper is used by meat packers, commercial bakers, pickle packers and condiment manufacturers.
